title: When Current Events Remain the Job of Single Departments, Kids Won’t Graduate Understanding the World Well standing-world-well/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that if current events live only in one department, such as English or a current-events elective, students will not graduate understanding the world, because understanding politics, climate or North Korea requires a body of knowledge no single course can build. He grounds this in his own classroom: a North Korea discussion was weak until three more articles of the week supplied the background, after which the same debate improved markedly. His conclusion is that knowledge begets critical thinking, not the reverse. He proposes two low-cost fixes: a monthly current-events graph in math, science or engineering classes using Kelly Turner's Graph of the Week, and a regular article of the week in social studies, ELA, health or business. Both should be lightly graded because the purpose is knowledge-building, and he closes by urging teachers to offer opportunities even if only half the students take them.
points: Critical thinking cannot be taught in the abstract; student reasoning on current issues improved only after they had read enough about the topic.
Building the knowledge for informed citizenship is a whole-school job, not the property of English or social studies departments.
A Graph of the Week in math and science classes takes about 15 minutes weekly and adds quantitative reasoning and writing practice alongside the knowledge-building.
Article of the week assignments should be graded in seconds, since their main purpose is knowledge, with reading and writing volume as a secondary benefit.
Teachers should not withhold good opportunities because only some students will complete them; the job is to provide opportunity, not guarantee results.
quotes: Kids (and adults!) won’t produce quality, clear thinking unless they know enough things. Knowledge begets critical thinking. Critically thinking is not immaculately conceived.

In order to understand things like US politics, global climate, the rise of automation, or the North Korea security and humanitarian crises, you need to know a lot of things, and such robust knowledge-building can’t happen in a single course or department. I don’t care how many times you talk to kids about critical thinking or how many times you have them argue or pop-up debate on the topics I just mentioned.
Here's the thing: it was my fault. I hadn't given my students a chance to learn enough about the North Korea situation yet.

The improvement was remarkable — students built on one another’s ideas, used Paraphrase Plus, and came much closer to matching what I had originally hoped for several weeks prior. Knowledge begot critical thinking and productive, argumentative discourse.

Something like this need only take 15 minutes maximum of class time each week, and it can take less once students are used to it. Importantly, grading on this should not be intensive. The primary purpose of the assignment is knowledge-building, and the secondary benefits include practice with quantitative reasoning, graph reading, and writing in the content areas.

Of course, there are also secondary benefits when we systematize the inclusion of regular current events articles: our students get the opportunity to read and write more. Since quantity precedes quality, this is no small boon.

Please notice that such ways of thinking devalue the 50% of students who would take advantage of an opportunity. This is something I hope my children's teachers never do, so it's something I won't do. You and I are in the business of providing opportunities, not guaranteeing results.
